lines: Chorus: each channel runs through a delay line whose time is moved by an internal sine LFO, and the delayed signal is mixed back with the dry one
Base delay time applied to each channel before the LFO moves it
EQ on the delayed signal: positive values thin and brighten it, negative values darken it
Depth of the internal sine LFO. Negative values move both channels by the same amount, positive values move them in opposite directions, 0° against 180°, which turns the stereo image
Frequency of the internal sine LFO that moves the delay time
How far the voltage at the DLY input moves the base delay time, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the TONE input moves the tone of the delayed signal, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the DEPTH input moves the modulation depth, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the RATE input moves the LFO frequency, and in which direction
Adds a third delay line to both channels, moved by a separate LFO at 120° phase: the tri-chorus, or ensemble, effect
CV over the base delay time
CV over the tone of the delayed signal
CV over the depth of the modulation
CV over the LFO frequency
External CV added to the modulation of the third delay line; with no cable here the MOD L signal drives it
External CV added to the modulation of the left channel
External CV added to the modulation of the right channel; with no cable here the MOD L signal drives both channels
Audio in; with no cable in RIGHT this signal feeds both channels
Right channel of the audio in

Right channel out, the dry and processed signals mixed
Menu — Invert left wet signal — inverts the left channel's processed signal before it is added to the dry signal, as some hardware does, which widens the stereo image
Flanger: each channel runs through a short delay line swept by an internal sine LFO, with feedback round the delay, and the result is mixed with the dry signal to make a moving comb filter
Base delay time applied to each channel before the LFO moves it. It also sets the note the flanger plays when it is driven as a voice, C5 by default
How much of the delayed signal is fed back into the delay line. A negative value feeds back an inverted signal, for a different tone, and an extreme value brings the flanger close to self-oscillation
Depth of the internal sine LFO. Negative values move both channels by the same amount, positive values move them in opposite directions, 0° against 180°, which turns the stereo image
Frequency of the internal sine LFO that moves the delay time
How far the voltage at the DLY input moves the base delay time, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the FDBK input moves the feedback, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the DEPTH input moves the modulation depth, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the RATE input moves the LFO frequency, and in which direction
Through-zero flanging: the dry signal is delayed by the base delay time as well, so the processed signal can arrive ahead of it through the negative half of the LFO cycle
CV over the base delay time
CV over the feedback
CV over the depth of the modulation
CV over the LFO frequency
Pitch at a volt per octave, for playing the near-self-oscillating flanger as a voice; set DEPTH to zero to lose the vibrato, and FDBK sets how long a note rings
External CV added to the modulation of the left channel

Phaser: each channel runs through a chain of all-pass filters whose cutoff is swept by an internal sine LFO, and mixing that with the dry signal puts moving notches through the spectrum
Base cutoff frequency of the all-pass filters. It also sets the note the phaser plays when it is driven as a voice, C5 by default
Feeds the filtered signal back into the start of the all-pass chain. A negative value feeds back an inverted signal, for a different tone; an extreme value nears self-oscillation
Depth of the internal sine LFO. Negative values move both channels by the same amount, positive values move them in opposite directions, 0° against 180°, which turns the stereo image
Frequency of the internal sine LFO that moves the cutoff
How far the voltage at the FREQ input moves the base cutoff, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the RES input moves the resonance, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the DEPTH input moves the modulation depth, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the RATE input moves the LFO frequency, and in which direction

Algorithmic reverb built from a chain of delays, filters and feedback loops. The display plots its impulse response: time left to right, frequency front to back, amplitude as the height of each line
Length of the reverb tail in seconds: roughly the time the reverberated signal takes to decay by -60dB
Character of the reverb, set by the mix of its internal delay taps
Cutoff of the high-pass filter inside the reverb, which keeps the reflections from turning muddy
Cutoff of the low-pass filter inside the reverb, which shortens the decay of the top end
How long the dry signal is delayed before the reverb processes it. In a room this is the time sound takes to reach the nearest wall and return, about 18ms for a wall 3m away
Stereo spread of the reverberated signal; at 0% it is mono, and it is then mixed with a dry signal that may be stereo
Balance between the dry input and the reverberated signal
How far the voltage at the TIME input moves the reverb time, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the MORPH input moves the character, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the HP input moves the high-pass cutoff, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the LP input moves the low-pass cutoff, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the WIDTH input moves the stereo spread, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the MIX input moves the dry and wet balance, and in which direction
Hold to freeze the reverb: its internal state is held and incoming audio is blocked, so the tail runs on without end

Convolution processor: the input is convolved with an impulse response, a recording of a space or of any other sound, loaded from a WAV file of as much as 60 seconds or recorded on the spot
Gain on the signal going into the convolution. Impulse responses are levelled by their root-mean-square as they load, and this trims the result
How much of the convolved audio is fed back in to be pre-delayed and convolved again. Past a point the loop runs away, so raise it a little at a time; the output is soft-clipped
Cutoff of the high-pass filter applied before the signal is convolved
Cutoff of the low-pass filter applied before the signal is convolved
How long the dry signal is delayed before it is convolved
Stereo spread of the convolved signal; at 0% it is mono, and it is then mixed with a dry signal that may be stereo
Balance between the dry input and the convolved signal
How far the voltage at the GAIN input moves the input gain, and in which direction
How far the voltage at the FDBK input moves the feedback, and in which direction

Menu — Load IR — picks the WAV file to convolve with; clicking the display does the same, and 26 impulse responses are shipped with the plugin
Menu — Reverse IR — plays the loaded impulse response backwards
Menu — Stretch — changes the length of the loaded impulse response and its pitch together
Menu — Save IR as — writes the loaded impulse response out to a WAV file
Note — Nothing reaches the wet path until an impulse response is loaded: click the display, use Load IR on the right-click menu, or hold the record button to capture one from the audio inputs
Stereo compressor with an optional sidechain, six models drawn from digital and analogue hardware, and metering of input, sidechain, gain reduction and output
Click to step through the meters, right-click to pick one: a scope of the last 2 seconds, an immediate linear reading from -48dB to +6dB, or a modelled VU meter from -20dB to +3dB
Rise time of the envelope follower that measures the level
Fall time of the envelope follower that measures the level
Level in dB at which gain reduction starts; audio below it is passed untouched
How sharply the ratio comes in around the threshold: at 0 it switches straight from 1/1 to the full ratio, and above 0 it moves across that many decibels
High-pass filtering from 10Hz to 1000Hz on the level detector, so sub-bass and bass energy do not pump the gain. The audio itself is not filtered
How hard audio above the threshold is pulled down: at 4/1 a 4dB rise going in gives 1dB coming out. Below 1/1 the module expands instead, and a 1dB rise gives more than 1dB out
Gain applied to the audio on its way in
Gain applied to the audio on its way out
Click to step through the six models, right-click to pick one: feed-forward, feedback, VCA, optical, FET and tube, each with its own character
Compensates for the gain reduction according to the threshold, so the loudness holds steady as the threshold is moved
Modulates the threshold: 10V leaves it where it is set, and lower voltages pull it down linearly
Audio the level detector measures in place of the audio input; the gain reduction it calls for is applied to the audio input all the same
Right channel of the sidechain audio
The audio that gets compressed; with no cable in the right audio input this signal is treated as mono
Right channel of the audio to be compressed
The gain reduction as a voltage: linear, 10V for none and 0V for full attenuation, so a linear VCA elsewhere can copy the reduction
Left channel of the compressed audio
Right channel of the compressed audio
Menu — GR output — switches the GR jack to Log, where 0V is no reduction, 1V is -6dB and 2V is -12dB, or back to Linear
Menu — Oversample — runs the models at 1x to 16x the sample rate, and is 2x unless changed
